Myszyniec Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Myszyniec, Poland

Demolished. Jews are first recorded in Myszyniec in the second half of the 18th century, with significant growth in the following century; population reached 48% (912) by 1921, before Germans expelled all Jews in 1939 - some reached Soviet territory, most others were later exterminated. This cemetery, established around 1850 (per an October 31, 1855 record noting the community self-funded a synagogue, study hall, bathhouse, and cemetery - previously burying dead in Ostrołęka), included a wooden fence and caretaker's building before the war. Postwar, the site became a sand mine: extraction destroyed graves and scattered bones, while locals dug for gold teeth and valuables; an electric line was later built through the grounds. A 2016 monument, initiated by Aharon Shachal with the Foundation for the Preservation of Jewish Heritage, reads 'The Jewish cemetery. The monument commemorates the Jewish inhabitants of Myszyniec, who were expelled from their homes during World War II. May their memory be a blessing.'
